reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: A single arterial trunk arises from the heart and gives rise to the coronary, pulmonary and systemic circulations, overriding a ventricular septal defect
A single truncal valve, often abnormal and regurgitant or stenotic, guards the common trunk
Complete mixing at the trunk produces mild cyanosis combined with heavy pulmonary overcirculation once pulmonary resistance falls
Untreated infants develop early heart failure and are at risk of rapidly progressive pulmonary vascular disease
There is a strong association with 22q11.2 deletion and the DiGeorge phenotype, warranting evaluation for immune and calcium abnormalities
Classification is based on how the pulmonary arteries branch from the common trunk
Early surgical repair separates the pulmonary arteries from the trunk, closes the ventricular septal defect and interposes a valved conduit to the pulmonary circulation
reference.pathophysiology: Truncus arteriosus results from failure of the embryonic truncus to septate into separate aorta and pulmonary artery, leaving a single great vessel overriding a ventricular septal defect and receiving output from both ventricles. Complete mixing of systemic and pulmonary venous blood occurs at the trunk, so arterial saturation reflects the ratio of pulmonary to systemic flow. As neonatal pulmonary vascular resistance falls, blood floods the pulmonary arteries, causing marked pulmonary overcirculation, torrential left-to-right shunting and congestive heart failure with only mild cyanosis. The frequently abnormal truncal valve may be regurgitant or stenotic, adding to ventricular loading. Persistent high pulmonary flow accelerates pulmonary vascular obstructive disease, which becomes irreversible if repair is delayed. The lesion is strongly linked to 22q11.2 microdeletion.
additionalDifferentials: Tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonary atresia and major aortopulmonary collaterals
Aortopulmonary window with ventricular septal defect
Transposition of the great arteries with ventricular septal defect
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography to demonstrate the single trunk, truncal valve, ventricular septal defect and pulmonary artery origins
Cardiac CT or MR angiography to define pulmonary artery and arch anatomy for surgery
Cardiac catheterisation to assess pulmonary vascular resistance when reversibility is uncertain
Genetic testing for 22q11.2 deletion with immune and calcium evaluation
Chest radiograph showing cardiomegaly and pulmonary plethora
redFlags: Early severe heart failure from unrestricted pulmonary overcirculation
Signs of advancing pulmonary vascular obstructive disease
Significant truncal valve regurgitation or stenosis with ventricular dysfunction
Hypocalcaemia, immune deficiency or coexisting interrupted aortic arch in the DiGeorge spectrum
reference.prognosis: Without surgery the outlook is poor because of early heart failure and irreversible pulmonary vascular disease; with early repair survival is good, though conduit replacement and truncal valve problems commonly require reintervention.
pitfalls: Delaying repair and allowing fixed pulmonary vascular disease to develop
Overlooking truncal valve dysfunction as a driver of ventricular failure
Missing associated 22q11.2 deletion with its hypocalcaemia and immune risks, including the need for irradiated blood products
Failing to detect a coexisting interrupted aortic arch
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
management: Undertake early complete surgical repair with ventricular septal defect closure and a right-ventricle-to-pulmonary-artery conduit
Control preoperative heart failure medically with diuretics and afterload reduction to limit pulmonary overcirculation
Repair or replace the truncal valve when significant regurgitation or stenosis is present
Screen for 22q11.2 deletion and manage hypocalcaemia and immunodeficiency, using irradiated CMV-negative blood products until immune status is known
Provide lifelong surveillance for conduit stenosis needing reintervention and for progressive pulmonary vascular disease
Give endocarditis prophylaxis and coordinate congenital cardiology follow-up
Offer genetic counselling in view of the strong 22q11.2 deletion association
